claim: Trait inference in social cognition relies on two universal dimensions: competence and warmth.
source: Such trait inference is thought to rely on two universal dimensions: competence and warmth.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established framework for understanding social cognition, drawing on existing literature.

claim: These two dimensions (competence and warmth) can be used to construct a 'social cognitive map' organizing massive information obtained from social encounters efficiently.
source: These two dimensions can be used to construct a 'social cognitive map' organizing massive information obtained from social encounters efficiently.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim stated in the abstract, based on the framework of social cognition.

claim: Participants were able to navigate to a learned location from random starting locations in the abstract social space.
source: Behaviorally, participants were able to navigate to a learned location from random starting locations in this abstract social space.
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the study reported in the abstract.

claim: Distance representation was identified in the precuneus, fusiform gyrus, and middle occipital gyrus.
source: At the neural level, we identified the representation of distance in the precuneus, fusiform gyrus, and middle occipital gyrus.
evidence: This is a neural finding from fMRI data reported in the abstract.

claim: Partial evidence of grid-like representation patterns was found in the medial prefrontal cortex and entorhinal cortex.
source: We also found partial evidence of grid-like representation patterns in the medial prefrontal cortex and entorhinal cortex.
evidence: This is a neural finding from fMRI data reported in the abstract.

claim: The intensity of grid-like response scaled with the performance of navigating in social space.
source: Moreover, the intensity of grid-like response scaled with the performance of navigating in social space and social avoidance trait scores.
evidence: This is a correlation finding reported in the abstract.

claim: The intensity of grid-like response scaled with social avoidance trait scores.
source: Moreover, the intensity of grid-like response scaled with the performance of navigating in social space and social avoidance trait scores.
evidence: This is a correlation finding reported in the abstract.

claim: The most widely recognized dimensions of social perception are warmth, which concerns others' intentions, and competence, which concerns others' capability and possession of resources.
source: The most widely recognized dimensions are warmth, which concerns others' intentions, and competence, which concerns others' capability and possession of resources (Cuddy, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cuddy, 2008.

claim: People ascribe a variety of traits to others, but these inferences rely on a few universal dimensions.
source: Though people may ascribe a variety of traits to others, these inferences have been identified to rely on a few universal dimensions (Fiske et al., 2007; Stolier et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fiske et al., 2007 and Stolier et al., 2020.

claim: Entorhinal grid cell activity supports representational coding of cognitive map in spatial navigation.
source: In the domain of spatial navigation, it has been demonstrated that entorhinal grid cell activity supports representational coding of cognitive map.
evidence: This is stated as an established finding in the spatial navigation literature.

claim: Direct recordings in rodents and humans have found that the firing locations of grid cells form periodic triangular patterns that cover the entire available arena during spatial navigation task.
source: Direct recordings in rodents (Hafting et al., 2005) and humans Jacobs et al., 2013 have found that the firing locations of grid cells form periodic triangular that covers the entire available arena during spatial navigation task.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hafting et al., 2005 and Jacobs et al., 2013.

claim: Grid cells form the basic units of a neural map of the spatial environment.
source: In this sense, grid cells form the basic units of a neural map of the spatial environment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of grid cells described in the literature.

claim: Neighboring grid cells share consistent grid orientation.
source: One of the prominent properties of grid cells is their consistent grid orientation (i.e., the orientation of the grid relative to the environment) shared by neighboring grid cells (Hafting et al., 2005; Sargolini et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hafting et al., 2005 and Sargolini et al., 2006.

claim: Entorhinal grid codes are capable of representing space at a higher level of abstraction that goes beyond spatial navigation to support cognitive flexibility in general.
source: Previous studies have suggested that entorhinal grid codes are capable of representing space even at a higher level of abstraction that goes beyond spatial navigation to support cognitive flexibility in general (Bellmund et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bellmund et al., 2018.

claim: Grid-like codes in EC and prefrontal cortex have been observed during nonspatial navigation such as perceptual, conceptual, semantic space, and discrete social hierarchy.
source: Grid-like codes in EC and prefrontal cortex (PFC) have been observed during nonspatial navigation such as perceptual (Aronov et al., 2017; Bao et al., 2019; Killian et al., 2012; Nau et al., 2018), conceptual (Constantinescu et al., 2016), semantic space (Viganò and Piazza, 2020; Viganò et al., 2021), and, more recently, discrete social hierarchy (Park et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating grid-like codes in various domains.

claim: The social value map was defined by two ecologically important dimensions: competence and trustworthiness.
source: We designed the social value map, an abstract social space structuring one's social perception of other people's social values. It was defined by two ecologically important dimensions: competence and trustworthiness.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Competence was operationally defined as the ability to earn a profit (profit rate) in an investment game.
source: We operationally defined these two dimensions under the framework of an investment game, in which the trustee's social value is determined by the ability to earn a profit (i.e., profit rate as competence) and the proportion of earnings returned to the investor (i.e., return rate as trustworthiness).
evidence: This describes the operational definition used in the study.

claim: Trustworthiness was operationally defined as the proportion of earnings returned to the investor (return rate) in an investment game.
source: We operationally defined these two dimensions under the framework of an investment game, in which the trustee's social value is determined by the ability to earn a profit (i.e., profit rate as competence) and the proportion of earnings returned to the investor (i.e., return rate as trustworthiness).
evidence: This describes the operational definition used in the study.

claim: Six avatars with different levels of competence and trustworthiness were placed on the social value map.
source: Six avatars with different levels of competence and trustworthiness (Figure 1A), analogous to landmarks in the physical environment, were placed on the social value map of size 1 unit × 1 unit in accordance with the range of competence and trustworthiness.
evidence: This describes the experimental design, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Participants were successful in reconstructing the designed layout of avatars in a map task at the end of the experiment.
source: Participants were successful in reconstructing the designed layout of avatars in a map task at the end of the experiment (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the study, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Participants took significantly less time to find all avatars in the review session compared to the learning session.
source: In the explore task, it took them significantly less time to find all avatars in the review session compared to the learning session (βsession = –67.589, t = –37.604, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from linear mixed effect models.

claim: Participants spent much less time at the edge during exploration in the review session compared to the learning session.
source: They also spent much less time at the edge (β = –0.104, t = –9.070, p<0.001) and more time at avatars (βsession = 0.023, t = 7.367, p<0.001) during exploration in the review session compared to the learning session (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a statistical result from linear mixed effect models, with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: Participants spent more time at avatars during exploration in the review session compared to the learning session.
source: They also spent much less time at the edge (β = –0.104, t = –9.070, p<0.001) and more time at avatars (βsession = 0.023, t = 7.367, p<0.001) during exploration in the review session compared to the learning session (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a statistical result from linear mixed effect models, with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: There was evident improvement in collect and recall task as training progressed.
source: Likewise, there was evident improvement in collect and recall task as training progressed (Figure 1F, percentage of first transition deviation < 15° in collect task: βsession = 0.050411, t = 3.2187, p=0.002; percentage of distance < 0.01 in collect task: βsession = 0.047, t = 3.002, p=0.003; accuracy in the recall task: βsession = 0.020, t = 4.213, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from linear mixed effect models, with reference to Figure 1F.

claim: There was a significant effect of distance between avatars in the compared dimension on response time and accuracy in the compare task.
source: In the compare task, linear mixed effect models revealed a significant effect of distance between avatars in the compared dimension on response time and accuracy as predicted (Figure 2G, all p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from linear mixed effect models, with reference to Figure 2G (note: this appears to be Figure 1G based on context).

claim: Learning induced changes in participants' ratings of avatars on all rating items (competence, trustworthiness, and attractiveness).
source: Lastly, learning-induced changes in participants' ratings of avatars on all rating items (competence, trustworthiness, and attractiveness) (Figure 2H, Table 1A).
evidence: This is a result from the study, with reference to Figure 2H (note: this appears to be Figure 1H based on context) and Table 1A.

claim: There was no preference over the six presented faces when participants were naïve to the social value of different avatars.
source: There was no preference over the six presented faces when participants were naïve to the social value of different avatars (Table 1B, all p>0.890), but their ratings became significantly dissociable according to the learned social value at the end of the experiment (Table 1B, all p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study, with reference to Table 1B.

claim: Participants' ratings became significantly dissociable according to the learned social value at the end of the experiment.
source: There was no preference over the six presented faces when participants were naïve to the social value of different avatars (Table 1B, all p>0.890), but their ratings became significantly dissociable according to the learned social value at the end of the experiment (Table 1B, all p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study, with reference to Table 1B.

claim: Activity in the bilateral precuneus positively correlated with traveled Euclidean distance.
source: This analysis revealed two marginally significant clusters in the precuneus whose activity positively correlated with traveled distance on the social value map (Figure 2A, Table 2A, right precuneus: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [12, –56, 26], t(37) = 4.952, p=0.056 FWE-corrected; left precuneus: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [-12, –54, 18], t(37) = 4.530, p=0.058 FWE-corrected; cluster-defining threshold p<0.001 FWE-corrected).
evidence: This is a result from whole-brain GLM analysis, with reference to Figure 2A and Table 2A.

claim: Negative correlation was observed between traveled distance and activity of clusters in bilateral fusiform gyrus.
source: Interestingly, we also observed negative correlation between traveled distance and activity of clusters in several regions, including bilateral fusiform gyrus (Figure 2B, Table 2B, right fusiform: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [36, –48, –20], t(37) = 5.912, p<0.001 FWE-corrected; left fusiform: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–38, –56, –10], t(37) = 4.724, p=0.008 FWE-corrected) and the right middle occipital gyrus (Figure 2B, Table 2B, peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [34, –68, 20], t(37) = 4.649, p=0.018 FWE-corrected; cluster-defining threshold p<0.001).
evidence: This is a result from whole-brain GLM analysis, with reference to Figure 2B and Table 2B.

claim: Negative correlation was observed between traveled distance and activity in the right middle occipital gyrus.
source: Interestingly, we also observed negative correlation between traveled distance and activity of clusters in several regions, including bilateral fusiform gyrus (Figure 2B, Table 2B, right fusiform: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [36, –48, –20], t(37) = 5.912, p<0.001 FWE-corrected; left fusiform: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–38, –56, –10], t(37) = 4.724, p=0.008 FWE-corrected) and the right middle occipital gyrus (Figure 2B, Table 2B, peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [34, –68, 20], t(37) = 4.649, p=0.018 FWE-corrected; cluster-defining threshold p<0.001).
evidence: This is a result from whole-brain GLM analysis, with reference to Figure 2B and Table 2B.

claim: Grid consistency effect was found in bilateral ventral medial PFC aligned to the right FP grid orientation.
source: For the right FP grid orientation, whole-brain analysis revealed consistency effect in bilateral ventral medial PFC (vmPFC, Figure 3D, left and middle panels, peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–14, 56, –12], t(37) = 4.245, cluster-level p=0.033 FWE-corrected, cluster-defining threshold p<0.005) and the left EC (left EC) extending to the parahippocampus (Figure 3E, left and middle panels, peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–16, –22, –26], t(37) = 4.563, cluster-level p=0.024 FWE-corrected, cluster-defining threshold p<0.005).
evidence: This is a result from whole-brain analysis of grid consistency, with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Grid consistency effect was found in the left EC extending to the parahippocampus aligned to the right FP grid orientation.
source: For the right FP grid orientation, whole-brain analysis revealed consistency effect in bilateral ventral medial PFC (vmPFC, Figure 3D, left and middle panels, peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–14, 56, –12], t(37) = 4.245, cluster-level p=0.033 FWE-corrected, cluster-defining threshold p<0.005) and the left EC (left EC) extending to the parahippocampus (Figure 3E, left and middle panels, peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–16, –22, –26], t(37) = 4.563, cluster-level p=0.024 FWE-corrected, cluster-defining threshold p<0.005).
evidence: This is a result from whole-brain analysis of grid consistency, with reference to Figure 3E.

claim: Significant consistency effect was found in two clusters in bilateral vmPFC aligned to the right pmEC grid orientation.
source: For the right pmEC grid orientation, significant consistency effect was found in two clusters in bilateral vmPFC (Figure 3F, left and middle panels, right rectus: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [10, 34, –18], t(37) = 4.908, cluster-level p=0.033 FWE-corrected; left ACC: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–8, 32, 6], t(37) = 4.810, cluster-level p=0.009 FWE-corrected; cluster-defining threshold p<0.005) and one cluster in right superior temporal pole (right STP, Figure 3G, left and middle panels, peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [36, 20, –30], t(37) = 4.962, cluster-level p=0.018 FWE-corrected, cluster-defining threshold p<0.005).
evidence: This is a result from whole-brain analysis of grid consistency, with reference to Figure 3F.

claim: Significant consistency effect was found in one cluster in right superior temporal pole aligned to the right pmEC grid orientation.
source: For the right pmEC grid orientation, significant consistency effect was found in two clusters in bilateral vmPFC (Figure 3F, left and middle panels, right rectus: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [10, 34, –18], t(37) = 4.908, cluster-level p=0.033 FWE-corrected; left ACC: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–8, 32, 6], t(37) = 4.810, cluster-level p=0.009 FWE-corrected; cluster-defining threshold p<0.005) and one cluster in right superior temporal pole (right STP, Figure 3G, left and middle panels, peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [36, 20, –30], t(37) = 4.962, cluster-level p=0.018 FWE-corrected, cluster-defining threshold p<0.005).
evidence: This is a result from whole-brain analysis of grid consistency, with reference to Figure 3G.

claim: The study did not identify grid-like pattern in EC that is aligned to the grid orientation of itself.
source: The above analysis did not identify grid-like pattern in EC that is aligned to the grid orientation of itself.
evidence: This is a null finding reported in the results.

claim: The study failed to find evidence of grid-like code in the EC aligned to its own putative grid orientation with the orientation estimation approach or with the RSA approach.
source: However, in the more statistically lenient ROI-based analysis, we failed to find evidence of grid-like code in the EC aligned to its own putative grid orientation either with this orientation estimation approach or with the representation similarity analysis (RSA) approach ('Materials and methods', Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a null finding reported in the results, with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: A clustered distribution of voxel-wise grid orientations was revealed in FP ROI for each participant.
source: This revealed a clustered distribution of voxel-wise grid orientations in FP ROI (V-test, all p<0.011, except in one participant's estimating set p=0.176; see Figure 3—figure supplement 3A for representative participants).
evidence: This is a result from V-test analysis, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Grid orientations across participants in the right FP ROI tend to distribute uniformly.
source: Previous studies using a similar approach in fMRI have also shown that grid orientations across participants tend to distribute uniformly (Bao et al., 2019). This has been replicated in the right FP ROI in our dataset (Figure 3—figure supplement 4, top, Rayleigh's tests for nonuniformity, all p>0.782).
evidence: This is a result from Rayleigh's test, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and citation to Bao et al., 2019.

claim: In the pmEC ROI, 31 participants show clustered distribution of voxel-wise orientations.
source: However, in the pmEC ROI, these results are less consistent. With regard to voxel-wise orientations, 31 participants show the above clustered distribution (V-test, all p<0.040; see Figure 3—figure supplement 3B for representative participants), but there are seven participants each of whom has at least one estimating set that did not pass the statistical test (V-test, all p>0.068).
evidence: This is a result from V-test analysis, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Across participants, only grid orientations from two estimating sets in pmEC ROI conformed to the uniform distribution.
source: Across participants, only grid orientations from two estimating sets conformed to the uniform distribution (Figure 3—figure supplement 4, bottom panel, Rayleigh's tests for nonuniformity, run 1,2,3: p=0.010, run 1,2,4: p=0.019).
evidence: This is a result from Rayleigh's test, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Signals within clusters showing significant hexagonal consistency were not modulated by any of the controlled periodicities (fourfold, fivefold, sevenfold, and eightfold).
source: One-sample t-tests showed that signals within these clusters were not modulated by any of the controlled periodicities, and paired t-test showed that sixfold periodicity in general showed greater alignment effect (Figure 3D–G, right panels).
evidence: This is a result from statistical tests, with reference to Figure 3D-G.

claim: Sixfold periodicity in general showed greater alignment effect compared to controlled periodicities.
source: One-sample t-tests showed that signals within these clusters were not modulated by any of the controlled periodicities, and paired t-test showed that sixfold periodicity in general showed greater alignment effect (Figure 3D–G, right panels).
evidence: This is a result from paired t-tests, with reference to Figure 3D-G.

claim: The vmPFC showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right FP's grid orientation.
source: In sum, our univariate analysis revealed that the vmPFC and left EC showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right FP's grid orientation and that the vmPFC and right STP showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right pmEC's grid orientation.
evidence: This is a summary of the univariate analysis results.

claim: The left EC showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right FP's grid orientation.
source: In sum, our univariate analysis revealed that the vmPFC and left EC showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right FP's grid orientation and that the vmPFC and right STP showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right pmEC's grid orientation.
evidence: This is a summary of the univariate analysis results.

claim: The vmPFC showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right pmEC's grid orientation.
source: In sum, our univariate analysis revealed that the vmPFC and left EC showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right FP's grid orientation and that the vmPFC and right STP showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right pmEC's grid orientation.
evidence: This is a summary of the univariate analysis results.

claim: The right STP showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right pmEC's grid orientation.
source: In sum, our univariate analysis revealed that the vmPFC and left EC showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right FP's grid orientation and that the vmPFC and right STP showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right pmEC's grid orientation.
evidence: This is a summary of the univariate analysis results.

claim: The study did not find correlation between hexagonal modulation effect and accuracy in the recall task in the scanner.
source: Previous studies have found that hexagonal modulation effect and hexagonal consistency effect positively correlate with accuracy in the recall task in the scanner (Constantinescu et al., 2016). However, we did not find such a correlation in our data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a null finding reported in the results, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citation to Constantinescu et al., 2016.

claim: Hexagonal consistency effect in the left middle temporal gyrus correlated with the distance effect in response time for grid orientation of right FP ROI.
source: For grid orientation of right FP ROI (Figure 4A), hexagonal consistency effect in the left middle temporal gyrus and right lingual gyrus correlated with the distance effect (left middle temporal gyrus: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–36, –70, 8], t(37) = 4.528, cluster-level p<0.001 FWE-corrected; right lingual gyrus: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–38, –66, 4], t(37) = 4.369, cluster-level p<0.001 FWE-corrected; cluster-defining threshold p<0.005).
evidence: This is a result from whole-brain analysis, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Hexagonal consistency effect in the right lingual gyrus correlated with the distance effect in response time for grid orientation of right FP ROI.
source: For grid orientation of right FP ROI (Figure 4A), hexagonal consistency effect in the left middle temporal gyrus and right lingual gyrus correlated with the distance effect (left middle temporal gyrus: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–36, –70, 8], t(37) = 4.528, cluster-level p<0.001 FWE-corrected; right lingual gyrus: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–38, –66, 4], t(37) = 4.369, cluster-level p<0.001 FWE-corrected; cluster-defining threshold p<0.005).
evidence: This is a result from whole-brain analysis, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Hexagonal consistency effect in bilateral lingual gyrus correlated with the distance effect for grid orientation of right pmEC ROI.
source: For grid orientation of right pmEC ROI (Figure 4B), hexagonal consistency effect in bilateral lingual correlated with the distance effect (left lingual gyrus: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–12, –68, –2], t(37) = 4.355, cluster-level p=0.077 FWE-corrected; right lingual gyrus: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [16, –62, –2], t(37) = 3.934, cluster-level p=0.032 FWE-corrected; cluster-defining threshold p<0.005).
evidence: This is a result from whole-brain analysis, with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Activities in the bilateral precuneus were positively correlated with traveled distance during mental traversal of a predefined social value map.
source: When participants were mentally traversing a predefined social value map, we found that activities in the bilateral precuneus were positively correlated with traveled distance, while activities in bilateral FFG and right MOG were negatively correlated with traveled distance.
evidence: This is a summary of the distance coding results in the Discussion.

claim: Activities in bilateral FFG and right MOG were negatively correlated with traveled distance during mental traversal of a predefined social value map.
source: When participants were mentally traversing a predefined social value map, we found that activities in the bilateral precuneus were positively correlated with traveled distance, while activities in bilateral FFG and right MOG were negatively correlated with traveled distance.
evidence: This is a summary of the distance coding results in the Discussion.

claim: Precuneus activity was positively correlated with traveled Euclidean distance during implicit navigation in the abstract social space.
source: Likewise, we showed that precuneus activity was positively correlated with traveled Euclidean distance during implicit navigation in the abstract social space.
evidence: This is a summary of the distance coding results in the Discussion.

claim: The current study's peak coordinates in precuneus coincide with those reported in a previous study by Park et al., 2020.
source: Moreover, the present peak coordinates coincide with those reported in a previous study by Park et al., 2020.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature, citing Park et al., 2020.

claim: Bilateral precuneus represented pairwise difference in the task-relevant dimension instead of pairwise Euclidean distance in the 2D space in Park et al., 2020 study.
source: In their study, participants learned 2D social hierarchy (competence and popularity) of two groups of agents and were asked to perform a transitive inference task in which they compared a pair of agents on their competence or popularity. The authors found that bilateral precuneus represented pairwise difference in the task-relevant dimension instead of pairwise Euclidean distance in the 2D space.
evidence: This is a description of findings from Park et al., 2020.

claim: Posterior cingulate cortex/precuneus tracks the length of the vector of social relationship change, that is, an egocentric distance.
source: Another study reported that posterior cingulate cortex/precuneus tracks the length of the vector of social relationship change, that is, an egocentric distance (Tavares et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of findings from Tavares et al., 2015.

claim: Precuneus may encode the distance of the route, either on a concrete or an abstract map, that participants trespass under task demand.
source: Taken together, we speculate that precuneus may encode the distance of the route, either on a concrete or an abstract map, that participants trespass under task demand.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings in the Discussion.

claim: The current study partly replicated findings of hexagonal modulated pattern in the EC and medial prefrontal regions aligned to putative grid orientation from both regions, with most findings in the prefrontal region.
source: Previous studies on reporting grid-like codes mostly report hexagonal modulated pattern in the EC and medial prefrontal regions aligned to putative grid orientation from both regions (Constantinescu et al., 2016). The current study partly replicated these findings, most of which are in the prefrontal region.
evidence: This is a summary of the grid-like code findings in the Discussion, with citation to Constantinescu et al., 2016.

claim: In terms of prefrontal orientation, whole-brain analysis revealed alignment effects in the bilateral vmPFC and left EC.
source: In terms of prefrontal orientation, whole-brain analysis revealed alignment effects in the bilateral vmPFC and left EC.
evidence: This is a summary of the grid-like code findings in the Discussion.

claim: In terms of entorhinal orientation, alignment effect was found in the bilateral vmPFC and right superior temporal pole, but not in the EC.
source: In terms of entorhinal orientation, however, alignment effect was found in the bilateral vmPFC and right superior temporal pole, but not in the EC.
evidence: This is a summary of the grid-like code findings in the Discussion.

claim: There has been no significant evidence of grid-like neuronal tuning in the prefrontal area to date.
source: To date, there has been no significant evidence of grid-like neuronal tuning in this area (Wikenheiser et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about the literature, citing Wikenheiser et al., 2021.

claim: Jacobs et al., 2013 examined grid-like cells in a variety of brain regions, including the frontal cortex in neurosurgical patients during a virtual navigation task, but the proportion of significant grid-like cells in the frontal cortex did not exceed type I error rate.
source: Jacobs et al., 2013 examined grid-like cells in a variety of brain regions, including the frontal cortex in neurosurgical patients during a virtual navigation task, but the proportion of significant grid-like cells in the frontal cortex did not exceed type I error rate (they did identify grid-like cells in cingulate cortex, which is posterior to the prefrontal regions).
evidence: This is a description of findings from Jacobs et al., 2013.

claim: It is less likely that the prefrontal grid-like codes reported in this study and previous literature come from grid cells in the PFC.
source: Therefore, it is less likely that the prefrontal grid-like codes reported in our study and previous literature come from grid cells in the PFC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of evidence for grid cells in PFC.

claim: A more plausible explanation is that the anatomically and functionally connected medial- and orbitofrontal cortex and EC coordinated together to support flexible decision-making.
source: A more plausible explanation is that the anatomically and functionally connected medial- and orbitofrontal cortex and EC (Navarro Schröder et al., 2015; Peng et al., 2018; Squire and Zola, 1996) coordinated together to support flexible decision-making.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation with citations to support anatomical and functional connectivity.

claim: The current study did not find reliable effect of hexagonal grid-like code in the entorhinal region aligned to its own grid orientation using both univariate and multivariate approaches.
source: However, adopting both univariate and multivariate approaches, the current study did not find the reliable effect of hexagonal grid-like code in the entorhinal region aligned to its own grid orientation, which should be evident if such hypothesis stands.
evidence: This is a summary of the null finding in EC.

claim: Previous studies postulated that the lack of univariate evidence of grid-like code may have to do with a low signal-to-noise ratio (tSNR) in data from the EC.
source: Previous studies postulated that the lack of univariate evidence of grid-like code may have to do with a low signal-to-noise ratio (tSNR) in data from the EC (Bao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about previous literature, citing Bao et al., 2019.

claim: Analysis revealed lower tSNR in all four entorhinal subregions compared to the frontal pole cluster from the quadrature filter analysis.
source: Indeed, analysis ('Materials and methods') revealed lower tSNR in all four entorhinal subregions compared to the frontal pole cluster from the quadrature filter analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is a result from tSNR analysis, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 5A.

claim: The study did not identify a significant relationship between tSNR and the Z-transformed F statistics of hexagonal modulation either across participants or within participants.
source: But we did not identify a significant relationship between tSNR and the Z-transformed F statistics of hexagonal modulation either across participants or within participants (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B and C, Table 4).
evidence: This is a result from correlation analysis, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 5B and C, and Table 4.

claim: The study cannot conclude that a low signal-to-noise ratio in EC led to the null finding.
source: Thus, we cannot conclude that a low signal-to-noise ratio in EC led to this null finding in our study.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the tSNR analysis results.

claim: The study provided some incomplete evidence of grid-like activity in the EC and prefrontal region while participants were mentally trespassing an abstract social space.
source: Nonetheless, our study did provide some incomplete evidence of grid-like activity in the EC and prefrontal region while participants were mentally trespassing an abstract social space.

claim: Park's study focused on discrete relational structures whilst the current study constructed a continuous social space.

claim: Evidence supports the notion that grid-like codes underpin navigation in an abstract social cognitive map, be it discrete or continuous.

claim: The intensity of hexagonal modulation in the precuneus aligned to estimated grid orientation of the prefrontal region is negatively correlated with participants' social avoidance tendency.
source: Intriguingly, our study found that the intensity of hexagonal modulation in the precuneus aligned to estimated grid orientation of the prefrontal region is negatively correlated with participants' social avoidance tendency.

claim: To the best of our knowledge, no report has shown the psychological relevance of grid-like code outside the EC and PFC to potential social deficit.
source: While previous studies mainly reported grid-like codes in the EC and PFC and its relevance to spatial navigation deficit in a clinically risky population (Kunz et al., 2015), to the best of our knowledge, no report has shown the psychological relevance of grid-like code outside these classical regions to potential social deficit.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding, with citation to Kunz et al., 2015.

claim: One study of direct neuronal recording revealed grid-like neuronal activity in patients' cingulate cortex during virtual spatial navigation task.
source: One study of direct neuronal recording revealed grid-like neuronal activity in patients' cingulate cortex during virtual spatial navigation task (Jacobs et al., 2013), implying that the human grid-cell network previously focused around the entorhinal and prefrontal regions also extends to the cingulate cortex.
evidence: This is a description of findings from Jacobs et al., 2013.

claim: The study did not find evidence of grid-like pattern in the precuneus.

claim: The study cannot conclude that the result points to a direct relationship between precuneus grid-like code and social functionality.
source: Thus, we cannot conclude that our result points to a direct relationship between precuneus grid-like code and social functionality.

source: Our findings further strengthen the notion that neural mechanisms involved in spatial cognitive map may play a domain-general role in maintaining an abstract, structured representation of knowledge that supports flexible cognitive behavior.

evidence: This is a speculation about the nature of social cognitive maps.

claim: Social ties are more likely to be formed among humans alike.
source: Social ties are more likely to be formed among humans alike (McPherson et al., 2001) and humans show the tendency to represent ingroup members more differentially than outgroup members (Hugenberg et al., 2010; Ostrom et al., 1993), so it is likely that some area of the social value space is represented in finer granularity than the other.
evidence: This is supported by citations to McPherson et al., 2001, Hugenberg et al., 2010, and Ostrom et al., 1993.

claim: Humans show the tendency to represent ingroup members more differentially than outgroup members.
source: Social ties are more likely to be formed among humans alike (McPherson et al., 2001) and humans show the tendency to represent ingroup members more differentially than outgroup members (Hugenberg et al., 2010; Ostrom et al., 1993), so it is likely that some area of the social value space is represented in finer granularity than the other.
evidence: This is supported by citations to McPherson et al., 2001, Hugenberg et al., 2010, and Ostrom et al., 1993.

claim: It is likely that some area of the social value space is represented in finer granularity than the other.

source: In this sense, spontaneous social value space may bear more resemblance to such kind of reward map covered by distorted grid fields rather than a regular, uniform square/circular open arena where sixfold symmetric grid-like coding was originally identified.

source: Our knowledge of other people in real life is often high-dimensional integrating multimodal information from sensory features (face, voice, etc.) to social cognitive information (hobbies, social status, etc.).
